lead: This unit explains how bearings carry loads with low friction, from lubricant choice to hydrodynamic journal bearings and rolling bearing life. After it you can compute film thickness, use the Sommerfeld number and Raimondi and Boyd charts, and select a ball or roller bearing for a required life.
about: The unit starts with lubricants (5.1): types and properties, with viscosity as the key number. Chapter 5.2 classifies sliding and rolling contact bearings and compares friction. Chapter 5.3 builds the hydrodynamic journal bearing: wedge action, clearance, eccentricity and minimum film thickness. Chapter 5.4 puts these variables into the dimensionless Sommerfeld number. Chapter 5.5 shows how the Raimondi and Boyd charts turn that number into film thickness, friction and oil flow. Chapter 5.6 moves to rolling bearings: dynamic load rating, equivalent load and L10 life. Chapter 5.7 uses those ratings to select a bearing from a catalogue and check static load and speed.

chapters.idea: A lubricant works by keeping surfaces apart; its viscosity, the resistance to flow, is the property that decides whether it can do that.
chapters.depth: Cover functions: reduce friction, carry away heat, protect from corrosion, seal gaps. Types: mineral oils, synthetic oils, greases (semi-solid lubricants), solid lubricants such as graphite and molybdenum disulphide. Properties: dynamic viscosity μ in Pa·s, kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ in m²/s (often cSt), viscosity index (VI), flash point, fire point, pour point, cloud point, oiliness, oxidation stability, emulsification. ρ is density. A high VI means viscosity changes less with temperature. Some syllabi call kinematic viscosity absolute viscosity divided by density. Mention SAE oil grades only as labels. Bearing design comes later.

figure.title: Lubricant choice
figure.aria: A flow from reducing friction through lubricant types and viscosity to property checks and grade selection.

chapters.example: An oil at 40°C has dynamic viscosity μ = 0.05 Pa·s and density ρ = 900 kg/m³. Find its kinematic viscosity in m²/s and in cSt. Solution: ν = μ/ρ = 0.05/900 = 5.56 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s. 1 cSt = 10⁻⁶ m²/s, so ν = 55.6 cSt.
chapters.trap: Using density in g/cm³ without converting, or swapping μ and ν. A common exam slip is to call 55.6 cSt equal to 55.6 Pa·s.
chapters.leave: Bearing pressure, clearance and life calculations to Chapters 5.3 to 5.7.

chapters.idea: Bearings are grouped by how surfaces move: sliding contact rubs, rolling contact uses balls or rollers, and each has its own friction and load limits.
chapters.depth: Sliding contact bearings: journal, thrust, bush, pivot, collar. Bearing materials: babbitt, bronze, cast iron; this completes the subject. Rolling contact bearings: ball, cylindrical roller, needle roller, tapered roller, spherical roller. Some syllabi call rolling bearings antifriction bearings. Compare friction, starting torque, load capacity, speed, noise, space and cost. Lubrication regimes: boundary (surfaces touch), mixed (partial film), hydrodynamic (full film). Do not derive film pressure or bearing life here.

figure.aria: A tree splits bearings into sliding contact with journal, thrust and bush types, and rolling contact with ball, roller and needle types.

chapters.example: A 100 mm diameter shaft carries a radial load W = 20 kN at n = 900 rpm. Compare friction power for a sliding bearing with μ = 0.02 and a rolling bearing with μ = 0.002. Use friction torque T = μ W d/2 and power P = Tω. ω = 2πn/60 = 94.25 rad/s. Sliding: T = 0.02 × 20 000 × 0.05 = 20 N·m; P = 20 × 94.25 = 1885 W. Rolling: T = 0.002 × 20 000 × 0.05 = 2 N·m; P = 2 × 94.25 = 188.5 W. The sliding bearing loses about 1.70 kW more.
chapters.trap: Using the shaft diameter instead of radius in T = μ W r, or putting rpm into P = Tω without converting to rad/s.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.1 for lubricant viscosity; Unit 1 for units and stress.
chapters.leave: Hydrodynamic pressure to Chapter 5.3; rolling bearing life to Chapter 5.6.

chapters.idea: In a hydrodynamic journal bearing, the rotating shaft drags oil into a narrowing gap, and the oil pressure built there carries the load without metal-to-metal contact.
chapters.depth: Geometry: journal diameter D, radius r, bearing length L, radial clearance c, eccentricity e, eccentricity ratio ε = e/c, minimum film thickness h_min = c(1 − ε). Attitude angle is the angle between the load line and the line of centres. Lubrication regimes: boundary, mixed, hydrodynamic. Wedge action, pressure distribution, oil grooves and oil supply. Starting and stopping wear. Reynolds equation only as the name; no derivation. Some syllabi call these fluid-film bearings. Use units: c and h_min have the same unit.

figure.title: Oil wedge action
figure.aria: A shaft turning drags oil into a converging gap; pressure builds and supports the load while a minimum film remains.

chapters.example: A journal bearing has D = 50 mm, radial clearance c = 0.05 mm, and eccentricity ratio ε = 0.6. Find eccentricity e and minimum film thickness h_min. Solution: e = ε c = 0.6 × 0.05 = 0.03 mm. h_min = c(1 − ε) = 0.05 × 0.4 = 0.02 mm = 20 μm.
chapters.trap: Using diametral clearance in place of radial clearance c. If a drawing gives clearance as 0.10 mm on diameter, then c = 0.05 mm. Also h_min is radial, not diametral.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.1 viscosity; Chapter 5.2 sliding contact classification.
chapters.leave: Sommerfeld number to Chapter 5.4; chart reading to Chapter 5.5.

chapters.idea: The Sommerfeld number puts speed, viscosity, load and clearance into one dimensionless group, so one set of charts can describe many journal bearings.
chapters.depth: Definition S = (μ n / p)(r/c)², where μ is dynamic viscosity in Pa·s, n is rotational speed in rev/s, p is bearing pressure W/(L D) in Pa, r is journal radius in m and c is radial clearance in m. Equivalent form S = μ n L D (r/c)² / W. n must be rev/s, not rpm. Some syllabi call S the bearing characteristic number. Higher S usually means lower eccentricity for the same L/D. Do not reproduce the charts here.

figure.aria: A straight line shows Sommerfeld number rising with speed; the marked point is the worked example at 25 rev/s and S = 0.03125.

chapters.trap: Putting n in rpm. The formula needs revolutions per second. Another trap is using πDL as the projected area; hydrodynamic bearing pressure uses L D.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.3 for clearance, eccentricity and film thickness.
chapters.leave: Raimondi and Boyd charts to Chapter 5.5; bearing selection to Chapter 5.7.

chapters.idea: Raimondi and Boyd charts convert the Sommerfeld number and length-to-diameter ratio into bearing performance: eccentricity, minimum film thickness, friction, oil flow and temperature rise.
chapters.depth: Design procedure: choose L/D (length-to-diameter ratio, often 0.5 to 1.5), find S, read ε from the chart for that L/D, compute h_min = c(1 − ε), read friction variable (r/c)f, compute f, torque T = f W r and power loss Tω. Read flow variable and temperature-rise variable; check oil viscosity at the operating temperature. Charts are empirical; interpolate between curves. Only a few universities teach the full temperature-rise iteration; treat it as a check.

figure.title: Reading the charts
figure.aria: A flow from Sommerfeld number and length-to-diameter ratio to eccentricity, minimum film thickness, friction and temperature check.

chapters.example: For the bearing of Chapter 5.4, S = 0.031 and L/D = 1. The chart gives ε = 0.62 and (r/c)f = 1.9. With c = 0.05 mm, r/c = 500, W = 10 kN and n = 25 rev/s, find h_min, friction coefficient f and power loss. h_min = c(1 − ε) = 0.05 × 0.38 = 0.019 mm = 19 μm. f = 1.9/500 = 0.0038. T = f W r = 0.0038 × 10 000 × 0.025 = 0.95 N·m. ω = 2π × 25 = 157.1 rad/s. Power = Tω = 0.95 × 157.1 = 149 W.
chapters.trap: Reading the chart at S in rpm or using the wrong L/D curve. Remember (r/c)f is not f; divide by r/c. Also h_min comes from radial clearance.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.4 for S; Chapter 5.3 for h_min.
chapters.leave: Rolling bearing life to Chapter 5.6; catalogue selection to Chapter 5.7.

chapters.idea: A rolling bearing's life falls as load rises; the basic dynamic load rating C and the equivalent load P give the L10 life in revolutions or hours.
chapters.depth: Basic dynamic load rating C in N is the load for a rating life of one million revolutions. Basic static load rating C0 is for non-rotating or slow loads. Equivalent dynamic load P = X F_r + Y F_a, where F_r is radial load, F_a is axial load, and X and Y are catalogue factors. Life L10 = (C/P)^p million revolutions, with p = 3 for ball bearings and p = 10/3 for roller bearings. Life in hours L10h = (10⁶/(60 n))(C/P)^p, with n in rpm. L10 means 10% failure probability or 90% reliability. Variable load and reliability adjustment only briefly.

figure.aria: The curve falls steeply; at 6 kN equivalent load the life is 125 million revolutions.

chapters.example: A deep-groove ball bearing has C = 30 kN. It carries P = 6 kN at n = 1500 rpm. Find L10 in million revolutions and in hours. L10 = (C/P)³ = (30/6)³ = 5³ = 125 million rev. L10h = 10⁶ L10/(60 n) = 10⁶ × 125/(60 × 1500) = 1389 h.
chapters.trap: Mixing N and kN in C/P, or using p = 3 for roller bearings. For hours, n must be rpm and the 10⁶ converts million revolutions to revolutions.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.2 rolling bearing types; Unit 2 fatigue idea.
chapters.leave: Bearing selection and static rating check to Chapter 5.7.

chapters.idea: Selection means calculating the required dynamic load rating from the load and life, then choosing a catalogue bearing with C at least that value and checking static load and speed.
chapters.depth: Procedure: find F_r and F_a; choose trial bearing type; find X, Y and the catalogue factor e; compute P = X F_r + Y F_a; choose required L10h; convert to L10 in million revolutions; C_req = P L10^(1/p); select a catalogue bearing with C ≥ C_req; check static safety C0/P0; check limiting speed and bore. Equivalent static load for many radial bearings: P0 = F_r or P0 = 0.6 F_r + 0.5 F_a, whichever is greater. Only a few universities teach reliability adjustment; keep it as a note. Do not name manufacturers.

figure.title: Bearing selection
figure.aria: A flow from loads to equivalent load, required life, required dynamic rating, catalogue choice and static and speed checks.

chapters.example: A deep-groove ball bearing carries F_r = 5 kN and F_a = 2 kN at n = 1200 rpm. The catalogue gives X = 0.56 and Y = 1.5 for F_a/F_r > e. Required L10h = 10 000 h. Find the required C. P = 0.56 × 5 000 + 1.5 × 2 000 = 2 800 + 3 000 = 5 800 N. L10 = 60 n L10h /10⁶ = 60 × 1200 × 10 000/10⁶ = 720 million rev. C_req = P L10^(1/3) = 5 800 × 720^(1/3) = 5 800 × 8.96 = 51 968 N ≈ 52 kN. Choose a bearing with C ≥ 52 kN.
chapters.trap: Using L10 in hours directly in C = P L^(1/3); convert to million revolutions first. Also forgetting to check C0/P0 and the limiting speed after the dynamic rating.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.6 for C, P and life.
chapters.leave: Bearing housing and shaft fits to Unit 3 shaft design; lubricant details to Chapter 5.1.
